grammar.title: Grammatik
grammar.rule: ich bin · du bist · er ist · sie ist · es ist · ich arbeite · du arbeitest · sie arbeitet
grammar.note_en:
A personal pronoun stands for a speaker, an addressee, or an already identified person or thing. Ich means “I,” the speaker. Du means “you” when speaking to one person informally. The reference changes with the speaker: when Lina speaks, ich means Lina; when Mira speaks, ich means Mira. Lina and Mira already use du with each other. Paul explicitly proposes informal address with Sagen wir du? (“Shall we use du?”), and Mira accepts with Ja, du (“Yes, du”). Learn this invitation as a fixed receptive phrase for now; its wir form is not a singular pattern to generalize or a required answer. The plural system comes next chapter, and formal address later. This establishes an invitation rather than assuming informal address with every unfamiliar person.

Er means “he” or “it” for a masculine singular noun; sie means “she” or “it” for a feminine singular noun; es means “it” for a neuter singular noun. Follow grammatical gender, not the usefulness or size of the object: der Koffer → er (“the suitcase → it”), der Stuhl → er (“the chair → it”), das Bett → es (“the bed → it”), das Zimmer → es (“the room → it”). Mira and Lina are referred to as sie. This chapter uses only singular personal pronouns; sie meaning “they” comes next chapter. These are subject forms, in the nominative. Object-pronoun case forms are not introduced here.

A finite verb changes with its subject. Sein (“be”) has special singular present forms: ich bin (“I am”), du bist (“you are”), er/sie/es ist (“he/she/it is”). Compare Ich bin heute hier (“I am here today”) and Du bist hier (“You are here”). The usual yes/no question puts the finite verb before the subject: Arbeitest du heute? (“Are you working today?”). To ask for confirmation, German can also keep statement order: Du heißt Mira? (“Your name is Mira?”). In speech, question intonation marks this use; here the question mark identifies it. In Wer bist du? (“Who are you?”), Wer comes first, followed by bist and the subject du. When the question word itself is the subject, it precedes the verb: Wer hat nicht viel Geld? (“Who does not have much money?”).

Many verbs use -e with ich, -st with du and -t with er/sie/es. The chapter shows ich lerne, du lernst, sie lernt (“I learn/study, you learn/study, she learns/studies”). Arbeiten inserts an extra e where pronunciation needs it: ich arbeite, du arbeitest, sie arbeitet (“I work, you work, she works”). Do not build du arbeitst. Present forms can describe a current activity, a routine, or an arrangement for later: Mira arbeitet morgen means “Mira works/is working tomorrow.” Morgen supplies the future context; German does not need a future auxiliary in this sentence. Heute means “today.”

Some frequent verbs change more than a regular ending. Haben gives ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat (“have/has”). Nehmen gives ich nehme, du nimmst, er/sie/es nimmt (“take/takes”). Sehen gives ich sehe, du siehst, er/sie/es sieht (“see/sees”). The tables collect the actual forms shown in the story. Earlier reading frames are now usable productively in the singular; this does not grant new tenses or plural endings.

The describing words after ist remain uninflected: Es ist groß (“It is large”), Es ist nicht leer (“It is not empty”). Viel Geld means “much/a lot of money”; nicht viel Geld means “not much money,” not no money at all. Geld is neuter and is used without an indefinite article here. Ich mache das Bett means “I make/straighten the bed,” as shown in the room scene. The arrangement gives Mira a bed today in return for work tomorrow; the furniture still has to be dealt with. No imperative or modal verb is needed in the sentences used to agree who takes which object.

Heißen (“be called”) has ich heiße (“I am called”) but du heißt (“you are called”), with no extra s before -t after ß: not du heißst. Compare Paul’s Du heißt Mira? (“You are called Mira?”) and Mira’s Ich heiße Mira (“I am called Mira”). The invitation and subsequent name check establish their mutual informal address before the lodging agreement.
